# Tame Your Inbox with Apple Intelligence in Mail

**By the end of this guide you'll be able to skim a long email in seconds and send a tidy, polite reply without typing the whole thing yourself. This is for anyone who uses Apple Mail on iPhone, iPad or Mac and wants to spend less time drowning in their inbox. Apple Intelligence is Apple's built-in AI assistant — think of it as a quiet helper that lives inside your apps and can read, write and tidy text for you.**

## Before you start

- **Device you'll need**: An iPhone, iPad or Mac that supports Apple Intelligence. In practical terms, that means an iPhone 15 Pro or newer, any iPhone 16, an iPad with an M-series chip, or a Mac with Apple Silicon (M1 or later). If you're unsure, open **Settings** and search for "Apple Intelligence" — if the toggle appears, you're good.
- **System version**: Update to the latest iOS, iPadOS or macOS before you start. The Mail features below live inside that update, not in a separate app you need to download.
- **iCloud sign-in**: You'll want to be signed into iCloud with a small amount of free storage available. No extra subscription is required for the Mail tools covered here.
- **Time**: About 5 minutes to set things up, then roughly 30 seconds per email once you're practiced.
- **One honest limit**: Apple Intelligence can summarize and rewrite, but it cannot send email for you. You always review and tap Send yourself — and you should, because the suggestions aren't perfect.

## Step 1 — Turn Apple Intelligence on

Open the **Settings** app on your iPhone, iPad or Mac. Scroll down and tap **Apple Intelligence & Siri** (on Mac this is under **Apple Intelligence** in System Settings). Toggle **Apple Intelligence** on if it isn't already. A short download begins — you'll see a status message like "Getting Ready…" while Mail's features are prepared, and then a confirmation that Apple Intelligence is ready to use. If you can't see that toggle at all, your device may not support Apple Intelligence; double-check the supported models in "Before you start". You'll know it worked when the setting shows a green tick and a welcome message appears on screen.

## Step 2 — Open Mail and find a long email

Open the **Mail** app from your home screen, Dock or Launchpad. Tap (or click) into your inbox and pick an email with more than a few paragraphs — a newsletter, a meeting recap or a long reply from a colleague works well. The full message opens with the sender's name at the top and the body of the email below. If your inbox is empty, send yourself a long block of text first, or wait for the next newsletter that lands. You'll know it worked when you can see the full email body and the standard Mail toolbar (Reply, Forward, Archive and so on) is visible.

## Step 3 — Let Mail summarize the email automatically

With the email open, scroll to the top of the message and pause for a second. Apple Intelligence automatically generates a short summary at the top of long emails — it appears as a couple of crisp sentences above the original text, with a small **"View Original Email"** link beneath if you want to see the full version. There's no button you need to press; the summary simply shows up. If you don't see a summary, the email may be too short to need one, or the feature may still be rolling out on your device — in that case, swipe down from the top of the email to refresh. On some devices you'll also see a brief summary directly under the email in your inbox list, before you even open it. You'll know it worked when a short, plain-English summary appears above the original text and the rest of the email sits neatly underneath.

💬 Example summary you might see: *"Anna is confirming Tuesday's meeting at 10am, sharing three agenda items, and asking you to review the attached budget before Friday."*

## Step 4 — Open Writing Tools inside your reply

Tap **Reply** as you normally would (the curved arrow at the top or bottom of the email). A new compose window opens with the original message quoted below. Place your cursor inside the empty reply area, then look for the **Writing Tools** option — on iPhone and iPad it's usually found by tapping the **Aa** formatting icon above the keyboard, then choosing **Writing Tools**; on Mac it's under **Edit → Writing Tools** in the menu bar. A small panel appears with options like **Rewrite**, **Proofread**, **Summary**, **Make Friendly**, **Make Professional** and **Make Concise**. If your screen looks different, look for an icon that resembles a pen with sparkles, or a small **⋯ menu** inside the compose window — Writing Tools sometimes hides there. You'll know it worked when a popup or floating bar appears with at least three tone and editing options.

## Step 5 — Tidy your reply with Rewrite, Proofread or a tone change

Start by typing a rough reply yourself — even just a few words is enough. Then choose a Writing Tool: tap **Proofread** to fix spelling and grammar, tap **Rewrite** to rephrase the whole draft, or pick a tone like **Make Friendly**, **Make Professional** or **Make Concise** to adjust how it sounds. Mail rewrites the text in place; the original sits underneath so you can compare. If the first rewrite isn't quite right, tap **Rewrite** again for a fresh take, or edit your draft first and try once more. The **Summary** option gives you a short version of what you've written — handy before you send a long reply.

💬 Example: type *"sounds good tuesday 10am works. can you send budget pdf"* then tap **Make Professional** and watch it become *"Tuesday at 10am works perfectly. Could you send the budget as a PDF when you get a chance?"*.

You'll know it worked when your reply text changes on screen and you can tap to swap between the original and the new version.

## Step 6 — Read, personalize and send the email yourself

Read the rewritten reply out loud once before sending — this is the most important step. AI suggestions aren't perfect, and you know things the AI couldn't (a colleague's nickname, an inside joke, a private detail). Add anything personal, double-check any names, dates or numbers, and make sure the tone sounds like you. When you're happy, tap **Send** exactly as you would for any normal email. Apple Intelligence never sends anything on your behalf — that's by design. You'll know it worked when your message lands in the Sent folder and the recipient gets a reply that sounds like you on a calm, well-rested day.

## Common mistakes

- **Mistake: Trusting the summary without checking.** Fix: Always glance at the original email if the summary mentions numbers, dates or money. AI summaries can occasionally drop a small but important detail.
- **Mistake: Sending the rewritten reply unchanged.** Fix: Read it once out loud. If it sounds stiff, robotic or oddly formal for the relationship, pick **Make Friendly** or **Make Concise**, or rewrite your draft first and try again.
- **Mistake: Looking for a Summarize button on every email.** Fix: Apple Intelligence only shows summaries when an email is long enough to need one. A one-line "Thanks!" message won't get a summary — and that's fine, just reply normally.
- **Mistake: Assuming it works on every device.** Fix: Older iPhones, iPads and Macs don't support Apple Intelligence. If the Writing Tools option is missing, check that your system is up to date and your device is on the supported list — otherwise the feature simply isn't available yet for you.

## What this means for you

- **In everyday life:** When a school newsletter or community group email lands in your inbox, you can get the gist in two seconds and reply in seconds, instead of saving it for "later" and never getting back to it.
- **For your business or work:** Long client updates, project recaps and meeting notes become three-sentence summaries, so you can triage your inbox in a fraction of the time and reply with a tidy, professional draft in seconds.
- **If you're just getting started:** Pick one email you haven't replied to yet and try the Summary + Writing Tools flow on it today. Treat the AI output as a starting point, not a final answer, and you'll get more comfortable with each reply.

## Try it now

Open Mail, find the longest unread email you have, scroll up to read the auto-summary, then tap **Reply → Aa → Writing Tools → Make Professional** on a rough draft you typed yourself. Read it out loud, tweak it, and send it. You'll have just triaged and answered an email in under a minute.
